reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Flail chest is defined by a segment of chest wall that has lost bony continuity, typically from multiple ribs each fractured in two or more places
The hallmark is paradoxical movement, where the flail segment moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration, opposite to the rest of the chest
The main threat to oxygenation is the underlying lung contusion rather than the chest wall movement itself
It is identified during the breathing step of the primary survey and demands close monitoring for respiratory deterioration
Adequate analgesia is central to management, allowing the patient to breathe deeply, cough, and clear secretions
Deterioration in gas exchange may require escalating respiratory support, including positive-pressure ventilation
Watch for associated injuries such as pneumothorax, haemothorax, and injury to underlying structures
reference.pathophysiology: When several adjacent ribs are each fractured in two or more places, an isolated segment of chest wall loses its bony connection to the rest of the thoracic cage. This segment then moves according to intrapleural pressure rather than muscular effort, producing paradoxical motion that reduces the efficiency of ventilation. More importantly, the force required to cause the injury bruises the lung beneath, and this pulmonary contusion impairs gas exchange, worsening over the first day or two. Pain from the fractures limits chest expansion and coughing, promoting atelectasis and retained secretions, all of which combine to cause hypoxaemia and, in severe cases, respiratory failure.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple rib fractures without a true flail segment
Sternal fracture with associated cardiac contusion
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph and CT to define rib fractures and pulmonary contusion
Arterial blood gas to monitor oxygenation and ventilation
Continuous pulse oximetry and respiratory monitoring
Assessment for associated pneumothorax or haemothorax
Serial evaluation as pulmonary contusion typically worsens over the first days
redFlags: Progressive hypoxaemia from evolving pulmonary contusion requiring escalation of respiratory support
Increasing respiratory distress and fatigue signalling impending failure
Associated tension pneumothorax or large haemothorax
Inadequately controlled pain preventing effective breathing and coughing
Signs of underlying great-vessel or cardiac injury
reference.prognosis: Outcome is largely determined by the severity of the underlying lung contusion and associated injuries. With good analgesia, chest physiotherapy, and respiratory support many patients recover, but extensive contusion and respiratory failure increase morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Focusing on the chest wall movement while underestimating the underlying lung contusion
Providing inadequate analgesia, leading to poor ventilation and secretion retention
Missing an associated pneumothorax or haemothorax
Assuming a stable early gas exchange will remain stable as contusion evolves
Excessive fluid administration worsening the pulmonary contusion
management: Aggressive multimodal analgesia, including regional techniques such as thoracic epidural or paravertebral blockade, to enable deep breathing, coughing and secretion clearance
Supplemental oxygen and escalating respiratory support, from non-invasive ventilation to intubation and positive-pressure ventilation for respiratory failure
Chest physiotherapy and pulmonary hygiene to prevent atelectasis and retained secretions
Surgical rib fixation of the flail segment in selected patients with severe deformity or ventilator dependence
Drainage of associated pneumothorax or haemothorax with an intercostal chest drain
Serial monitoring of gas exchange and clinical status, anticipating that the underlying pulmonary contusion worsens over the first days
Trauma and critical-care involvement with close observation for respiratory deterioration
